title: Project on Theatre Programmes
subject: listening

paragraphs.text: MAYA: So Finn, I’ve done as much as I can for our project on theatre programmes. How’s your research coming along?

FINN: OK, Maya. I didn’t know theatre programmes are called playbills in the USA till I started looking into the topic. Even though I struggled to find many useful websites, I’m glad we picked this subject. No one else on the course is doing the same as us, although it is one of the research areas of the module convenor.
MAYA: That might actually put some people off.
FINN: I suppose so. Anyway, I hadn’t realised there are actually companies specialising in creating theatre programmes.

MAYA: Yes, they’re quite common nowadays. Contrary to what many people think, theatres don’t hire people to do the programmes, in fact companies buy the rights to publish programmes on the theatre’s behalf – and then make their money selling advertising space within the programme booklet.
FINN: It must be easier for theatres to do it that way.
MAYA: Yes.
FINN: I remember reading something about programmes in early British theatre. It said that the cast was always very important.
MAYA: Yeah, audiences were very familiar with leading actors, and big names would draw huge crowds.

FINN: But I hadn’t realised that if the programme named a famous actor, that’s who the public expected to perform. And if that didn’t happen, people accused the theatre of breaking their agreement with the audience. They would demand refunds, and, if they didn’t get them, there were riots!
MAYA: Outrageous. That’d never happen now.
FINN: No, people are too polite, even when they’re disappointed if the star of the show misses a performance.

MAYA: We should definitely include that information about early audiences in our project. I also think it’s important to mention that lots of ordinary people at that time were illiterate, so theatre programmes were of limited value in advertising plays. When a company of actors arrived in a town, they’d parade around the streets in their costumes, beating drums and announcing their upcoming performances.
FINN: Interesting. I couldn’t imagine that happening now either.
MAYA: There’s also an interesting comparison to make between eighteenth and nineteenth-century programmes.
FINN: Wasn’t it in the nineteenth century that theatre programmes started to resemble programmes today?
MAYA: Yes. And, unlike programmes from the eighteenth century, they always used colour.
FINN: And there was a greater variety of designs. But personally, I think eighteenth-century programmes were superior because they told the theatre-goers so many things, including about the actors.
MAYA: And about the writer, the plot, and sometimes the history of the play.
FINN: That’s right. … What should we say about theatre programmes in the twentieth century?
MAYA: I reckon the most important thing is the dramatic change they underwent during World War Two.
FINN: When the government imposed restrictions on the use of paper.
MAYA: Yeah, but that was only in the UK. In the USA, programmes – or rather, playbills – continued to be published in the same format …
FINN: … while here in the UK, programmes became merely a single sheet of paper folded to create four pages for text.

MAYA: What I don’t really get is that, after the war, they didn’t go back to being more than one sheet, or change in any way for over twenty-five years. I know there were paper shortages after the war, but only for five or ten years.
FINN: Strange.
MAYA: I’ve got some pictures of programmes we could include on the slides for our presentation.
FINN: I found a couple too, Maya. Let’s go through and see what we think.
MAYA: Erm …, this is an old one, for a play called Ruy Blas.
FINN: Never heard of that, but the programme looks very decorative.
MAYA: Good enough to put in a frame on the wall. The images are just beautiful. Finn, what did you find?

FINN: I’ve got some pages from a programme for Man of La Mancha. I thought this was a good programme to show, not because of the pictures, but because it contains articles written by members of the theatre company. So we can learn how the production was created, and the thoughts and feelings of the cast.

MAYA: Good. I’ve got a copy of a programme that’s now in a museum. It’s for The Tragedy of Jane Shore and it’s said to be the earliest surviving document to have been printed on Australia’s first printing press.
FINN: Fantastic.

MAYA: Another programme to talk about is for The Sailors’ Festival. It comes from the British Library’s digitised collection of programmes that was started a few years ago. It already comprises over two hundred thousand programmes, which is amazing.
FINN: Wish I’d known about it while I was doing my research!

Questions 21–26

Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Finn was pleased to discover that their topic

options.text: was not familiar to their module leader.
had not been chosen by other students.
did not prove to be difficult to research.

questions.explanation: 录音原文中Finn所述内容里，先提及Even though I struggled…看似与C选项的difficult有关联，但未体现选项中的not prove，排除C。之后原文中的glad，对应题干的pleased。紧跟着原文中的no one else on the course以及doing the same，对应B选项。另外，原文还提及module convenor，与A选项中module leader有关，但相关原文中one of the research areas与选项中not familiar不符，排除A选项。因此本题答案为B。

questions.prompt: Maya says a mistaken belief about theatre programmes is that

options.text: theatres pay companies to produce them.
few theatre-goers buy them nowadays.
they contain far more adverts than previously.

questions.explanation: 在原文中Finn先提及没有意识到there are actually companies specialising in creating theatre programmes，但与题干的Maya不符合。接下来Maya所述内容里，先讲到与很多人所认为的不同，其中contrary to sth表示“与之相异的，相反的”。Maya紧接着提及的情况是theatres don’t hire…，本句中的contrary、what many people think以及don’t可以表现出题干里的mistaken belief。原文中还进一步讲到实际情况是companies buy the rights to publish以及on the theatre’s behalf，也就是说公司代表（或代替）剧场购买版权来发行，on sb’s behalf或on behalf of sb表示“代表（或代替）某人”，而这些公司是通过售卖节目手册中的广告版面来获利的。因此人们误以为的情况对应A，即本题答案。

questions.prompt: Finn was surprised that, in early British theatre, programmes

options.text: were difficult for audiences to obtain.
were given out free of charge.
were seen as a kind of contract.

questions.explanation: 原文中Finn所述内容里，题干的early British theatres和programmes原词重现，接下来Maya提及audiences。然后Finn说到的hadn’t realised对应题干的surprised，原文中agreement对应C选项的contract。这段话中还讲到who the public expected to perform，“公众期待进行表演的演员”，之后讲到breaking their agreement，“违反他们的协议（或契约）”，以及demand refunds，“要求退款”，这些能够整体反映出C选项表达的意思“被看作是一种合约（或契约）”。因此本题答案为C。

questions.prompt: Maya feels their project should include an explanation of why companies of actors

options.text: promoted their own plays.
performed plays outdoors.
had to tour with their plays.

questions.explanation: 原文中Maya所述内容里讲到，对于宣传戏剧来说，剧场节目单的作用是有限的，这里的advertising plays已经与A选项内容相关。之后原文中a company of actors对应本题题干的companies of actors，接下来的原文中的parade around the streets、beating drums以及announcing their performances，都表现出了演员们的宣传推广行动。因此本题答案为A。

questions.prompt: Finn and Maya both think that, compared to nineteenth-century programmes, those from the eighteenth century

options.text: were more original.
were more colourful.
were more informative.

questions.explanation: 本题题干中的nineteenth-century programmes和the eighteenth century，在原文中都原词重现，但需要注意本题重点在于the eighteenth century相关内容。原文中colour所在句中，通过unlike…the eighteenth century，可以排除B选项。后来在Finn所述内容中，关于18世纪节目单的表述是told the theatre-goers so many things，加上about the actors，都可以看出节目单提供了很多信息，加上Maya进一步作的补充writer、plot和history，两位的表述都对应C选项的informative，意为“提供有用信息的，给予知识的”。因此本题答案为C。

questions.prompt: Maya doesn’t fully understand why, in the twentieth century,

options.text: very few theatre programmes were printed in the USA.
British theatre programmes failed to develop for so long.
theatre programmes in Britain copied fashions from the USA.

questions.explanation: 本题题干中的the twentieth century在原文中原词重现，原文中UK对应选项里的British和Britain，原文中Maya说到的don’t really get对应题干里的doesn’t fully understand。原文中didn’t…change和over twenty-five years，分别对应B选项的failed to develop和so long。因此本题答案为B。
